claims.claim: Cohen and Bradford's Influence Without Authority (1991, third edition 2017) is based on reciprocity; its steps are assume all are potential allies, clarify goals and priorities, diagnose the other's world, identify currencies, deal with relationships, influence through give and take; currencies are grouped as inspiration, task, position, relationship and personal; negative currencies are a last resort.
claims.source: Newswise on the third edition, Cohen and Bradford's article reprinted by the University of Washington, and secondary summaries, found by search on 13 November 2026; the book is in the course owner's NotebookLM notebook but was not queried from the build environment.

concept_html:
Most of what a data platform needs sits with people you do not manage: the HR system owner who must add a field, the security team who must approve access, the finance lead who funds capacity. You cannot order them. You can trade.

The exchange model. Allan Cohen and David Bradford's Influence Without Authority (first edition 1991, third edition 2017) rests on reciprocity: people help those who help them. You influence by giving something the other person values in exchange for what you need. The authors set it out as steps:

  1. Assume everyone is a potential ally, including the person blocking you.
  2. Clarify your goals and priorities. Know what you need most, and what you can let go.
  3. Diagnose the other person's world: their goals, pressures and how their performance is judged.
  4. Identify the currencies they value and the ones you hold.
  5. Deal with the relationship. Trust makes every exchange easier.
  6. Influence through give and take.

Currencies. The book groups what people value into five kinds:

  • Inspiration: a vision, doing the right thing.
  • Task: resources, help, information, faster results.
  • Position: recognition, visibility to senior people, reputation.
  • Relationship: being understood, belonging, personal support.
  • Personal: gratitude, ownership, feeling competent.

An example. The HR system owner has no reason to add a change-notification field for you. Their world: a backlog and a monthly board report built by hand. Offer to automate that report from the platform (task), and credit their team when you present it (position). Now the field serves their goals too.

Avoid negative currencies, such as escalating over someone's head. Use them only as a last resort.

lines: Before asking: their team rebuilds the monthly headcount report by hand
and is judged on backlog size.
I could automate your monthly headcount report from the platform. It needs
a change-notification field on the employee table, which would also feed
our data quality checks. Could we look at it together this week? I will
credit your team when we present the platform to the CHRO.

notes.html: Diagnosing their world first: their pressure and how they are judged.
A task currency they value, offered before the ask.
A position currency: visibility to senior people.

example.takeaway_html: Diagnose what the other person values, offer currencies they care about, such as task help or visibility, and trade for what you need. Keep escalation for the last resort.

notes.html: Your priority, not theirs. Nothing in it is something they value.
A threat of escalation, a negative currency, used first instead of last.

title: Influence without authority
why_html: A data engineer asked the payroll system owner three times for an extract and escalated twice. Each escalation made the owner less willing. A colleague asked what was overloading the payroll team, offered to take over a quarterly reconciliation they hated, and had the extract in a week.
